headline: A Democratic sweep of the US midterms dominated the day. Stocks and Treasurys steadied after a jittery start, oil and the dollar eased, and the AI trade is being reassessed. Novo, CVS and Pfizer all lifted guidance, and Anthropic's IPO filing is drawing scrutiny.

paragraphs.text: Big healthcare earnings leaned positive. The Journal reports CVS raised full-year guidance on stronger health-care benefits and pharmacy results, though it stayed cautious about costs and the macro backdrop. The same news cycle says CVS will split in two, separating retail pharmacies from the insurance and pharmacy-benefit businesses. The reports in the list are brief, so timing and structure are unclear. Novo Nordisk raised its forecast on strong uptake of the Wegovy pill, with the FT and MarketWatch noting demand for GLP-1 products above expectations and a jump in the shares. Endpoints puts the guided sales growth at roughly flat, which it calls an upgrade for Novo, and notes the finance chief is leaving. Fierce says Novo booked billions in impairments after recent clinical misses, and the CEO is still looking for deals to fill pipeline gaps. Pfizer also raised 2026 guidance and beat third-quarter estimates, helped by Eliquis and 37% growth from acquired products, which offset the decline in Covid sales.

paragraphs.text: Licensing activity stayed brisk, much of it involving Asian assets. Bloomberg says Boehringer Ingelheim signed a deal potentially worth more than $7 billion with China's Sino Biopharmaceutical for experimental cancer drugs. AbbVie is paying $100 million upfront, with up to $1.37 billion in milestones, for Nxera's EP4 agonist program in inflammatory bowel disease. Shanghai-based Minghui is getting $110 million upfront for Japanese rights to a Phase 3 thyroid eye disease drug. Rhythm and LG Chem rewrote their oral obesity license, lifting scheduled payments to as much as $855 million from $305 million. For dealmakers, the pattern is large headline values and modest upfronts, with China-sourced assets prominent. Bit.bio also raised a $25 million Series D.

paragraphs.text: The pipeline news was mixed. Servier's $1.55 billion Edgewise acquisition took a hit when sevasemten failed its pivotal trial on primary and secondary endpoints, according to Endpoints and STAT, a costly early outcome for the buyer. Ultragenyx is cutting 20% of staff, dropping a Wilson disease gene therapy and halving R&D spend from the 2025 level. Sanofi ended a Nurix STAT6 degrader two months after it entered the clinic, and Novartis walked away from its BioArctic collaboration. AbbVie dropped a Phase 2 solid-tumor antibody, and Pfizer axed a Phase 2 pulmonary hypertension program and pared its obesity pipeline. On the positive side, Madrigal's Rezdiffra passed $1 billion in annual sales and Inovio won FDA approval for Voceryq. Vertex also tried to calm fears ahead of an FDA decision on its IgA nephropathy drug.

paragraphs.text: On policy, STAT says Democratic control of the Senate gives them power to push back on Trump's health care moves. Pfizer's Albert Bourla told Endpoints he expects no change to the most-favored-nation pricing deals struck with the White House. Endpoints is hosting a live discussion on the biopharma implications this afternoon. Separately, KFF finds Medicare Part D premiums could rise about 50% on average next year for people who do not switch plans. The NYT reports insurers are frequently withholding payments under the surprise-billing law. UnitedHealthcare will drop prior authorization on more than 2,000 pediatric codes from Dec. 1, and the FTC sent warning letters to 25 insurer marketing firms as ACA enrollment opens. Among providers, MultiCare and Samaritan closed their merger with a $700 million investment pledge, while Mass General Brigham staff are anxious after layoffs. Philips set aside $322 million for a proposed DOJ settlement over its sleep apnea recall. Public health news included New York's first fatal measles case in 30 years, with US cases nearing 5,000.

paragraphs.text: The Democratic landslide in the midterms set the tone. The FT and the Journal report Democrats took Congress, and Trump conceded the Iran war was partly to blame for the Republican losses. Markets first sold off, then recovered. The NYT says global markets fell on early results and later traded higher, and the FT says US futures reversed early losses as analysts argued divided government lowers policymaking risk. The Journal and Bloomberg describe equities and Treasurys rallying once the political picture was clear. CNBC separately noted Treasury yields fell overnight as investors sought safety during the equity futures sell-off, so the first move was a flight to bonds rather than a cheer. European stocks extended gains, led by renewables and banks, while Asian stocks recovered early losses as AI worries eased. Defense is the clear loser: European defense shares slid on expectations of less US military spending growth. Tesla and SpaceX fell premarket after a defeat for Republicans Musk had funded, including the $47 million the FT says he put behind Ken Paxton's Texas Senate bid, which Talarico won.

paragraphs.text: The AI trade is the main thing being reassessed. UBS expects renewed volatility in tech but not a derailing of the investment cycle. Goldman's strategist argues the status quo may push companies to speed up compute expansion rather than risk new rules in 2029. The FT, however, reports Democratic governors were elected on promises to halt data-centre building in Texas, Georgia and Ohio. Company news was supportive: AMD, Super Micro and Palantir were all in focus on AI demand, though Palantir dipped despite bullish analysts, and Apple and Shopify fell after their results on margin and revenue worries. Google plans to invest $15 billion in Malaysia over 2027 and 2028. CNBC's Santoli says the bull market probably needs tech to recover to advance.

paragraphs.text: Oil fell as investors weighed the election and Iran risk. Deutsche Bank analysts said prices would face more downward pressure if Middle East escalation stays absent, while European gas rose as traders waited to see whether Trump pursues diplomacy or new strikes. The Journal also notes Iran is using guerrilla tactics against oil flows through Hormuz. Gold climbed on a softer dollar and lower Treasury yields. Aramco's third-quarter profit rose 9% despite attacks on pipelines and refineries, and Mitsui's chief warned geopolitical risks are unpredictable rather than calming. The FT also reports a widening crisis at refiner Heraeus over alleged platinum test manipulation.

paragraphs.text: Inflation and central banks remain the macro counterweight. Eurozone inflation hit 4% in October, double the ECB's target and the fastest in three years, driven by energy; the euro held its gains with little reaction. Swiss inflation rose to 1.5%. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates 25 basis points to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, and Bank of Canada's Macklem pledged care on further hikes after moving to 2.5%. New Zealand unemployment rose to 5.7%, and the PBOC raised the FX reserve requirement by two points to 6% to steady the yuan. In the US, job openings and quits rose in September, supporting the Fed's resilient-labor narrative. The FT is also profiling frontrunners to succeed Lagarde at the ECB.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac rallied as Bill Ackman argued the midterms could help their exit from conservatorship. The $6.3 billion Binance hack has put crypto custody in focus, with the company saying it will reimburse customers. Corporate results were uneven: Continental, Pandora and Harley-Davidson were upbeat, while Ahold Delhaize cut its forecast after a cyber attack, BMW downgraded targets for the second time since June, and Volvo Car sales fell 16%.

paragraphs.text: Credit coverage today was thin on hard data but consistent in tone: calm headline spreads, with stress building underneath. Real Investment Advice describes spreads as calm on the surface with concern at the bottom, and Hedgeweek says hedge funds are warning of mounting private-credit risks as refinancing pressure grows. Both reports are brief in the list, so specifics are limited.

sources.title: Credit Spreads: Calm On The Surface, Concern At The Bottom

paragraphs.text: The sharpest example is in London. The FT reports that Arini Capital Management, run by Hamza Lemssouguer, has been caught in a brutal sell-off in the riskiest parts of corporate debt. It went from start-up to Mayfair mainstay in four years and is now fighting to hold on to its bets. The coverage ties the losses to a swashbuckling trading style. It is a reminder that concentrated positions in the weakest credits can unwind quickly when liquidity thins, though the list gives no sign of broader contagion.

paragraphs.text: The AI buildout is the other credit theme. Blackstone president Jon Gray said AI infrastructure needs more equity as debt investors face concentration risks amid huge spending plans. FT Alphaville says AI is making credit default swaps useful again, presumably as a hedging tool for exposure to heavily indebted AI names. The FT's opinion pages also ask whether markets are ready for an AI bust, arguing the longer the investment surge and its financial engineering last, the bigger the damage when it ends.

paragraphs.text: On the distress side, Karyopharm filed Chapter 11 with Ayrmid lined up as lead bidder in a court-supervised auction, per Fierce Pharma. The NYT says soaring diesel costs are pushing small trucking firms toward bankruptcy because they have little margin for error. In private credit, one report says India's private credit assets under management could triple to $65 billion by 2030, and Kalkine looks at an ASX-listed trust mixing private credit, royalties and water. South Korea's Lunit swapped 8% high-yield convertible bonds for 4% notes in a new 47.7 billion won issue, a refinancing that lowers its coupon.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO filing is the biggest capital-markets story, and the list has only commentary. Fortune says the filing shows that Dario Amodei's vision of a country of geniuses in a data center depends on risky financial mechanics. Morningstar expects the IPO to cast a long shadow over private AI stocks, and the FT's editorial board sees an opportunity to rethink IPO rules. Details of size, valuation or timing are not in the list, so treat the read-across as opinion for now.

paragraphs.text: Elsewhere, IPO appetite looks uneven. Reuters and Finimize report Chinese chipmaker YMTC has put its Shanghai IPO on hold as weaker markets weigh, according to sources. Malaysia's KEB drew a lukewarm response and was barely oversubscribed, per the Malaysian Reserve. Encube Ethicals has started investor meetings for a possible November IPO. On the strategic side, Lonza is buying Merck KGaA's US-based CDMO network for a mid-triple-digit million euro price, adding five sites and exposure to cell and gene therapy and viral vectors. Bank of America warned Marvell could fall sharply after its acquisition of Lumentum, and Bilt agreed to a $300 million deal for sports loyalty firm Lava. LeanTaaS is acquiring LookDeep Health.
